title: Ultrarare Nintendo Cartridges Found After Years in Storage
paragraphs: A box of old video games that had been sitting in storage for years has turned out to contain some extremely rare and valuable Nintendo cartridges.

The discovery was made in Waukesha, Wisconsin, near Milwaukee. Kevin Braun, the owner of a pop culture store called One Stop Wonders, had a box of Super Mario Bros. cartridges that he had bought from a customer. The customer's family had kept them for scrap metal and did not believe they were worth much. When Braun asked Jason Ganos, a well-known Nintendo collector and the publisher of the news website Nintendo Wire, to help him sell some other items, he mentioned the box.

The box contained 97 unused copies of "Super Mario Bros./Duck Hunt," a game bundle for the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES), and Ganos described them as absolutely pristine. The bundle was first released in 1988 and discontinued in 1991. However, Ganos discovered that these cartridges had been made in 1993. This meant that they were not only a previously unknown version of the game, but also the last known copies ever produced. Braun and Ganos are still not sure why they were made, but they believe the cartridges may have been warranty replacements or part of a deal with a retailer that never happened.

The cartridges were then examined by Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA), a company that grades the condition of collectibles. Remarkably, five of the 97 cartridges received a perfect score of 10. According to Ganos, an NES cartridge had never received a perfect score before. Ganos compared the find to pulling out a "Holy Grail."

Three of the cartridges with perfect scores were put up for sale at an online auction that ran until September 9, 2026, along with most of the others. Braun and Ganos decided to keep one perfect-scoring cartridge and several others. They also plan to hold a charity auction later.

Ganos refused to estimate how much the cartridges might be worth. He said they could sell for hundreds, thousands or even tens of thousands of dollars. However, he believes that their perfect condition could raise their value, as it does for comic books and sports cards. Rare video game cartridges have sometimes sold for very large sums in the collector's market.
